surpass

sur-PASS -- built from 'sur-' (over, beyond) plus 'pass.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To surpass is to become greater, better, or more successful than a rival, a record, or what was expected.

This year's fundraiser is expected to surpass last year's total by a wide margin.

Worked Example

A young runner shatters the school's decades-old track record, finishing the race nearly two full seconds faster than anyone ever had before.

That clear exceeding of a previous standard or rival is exactly what surpass means. Unlike 'match,' which means to equal something, surpass means going beyond it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

outdo: To outdo is to do better than a rival at the same activity, often with a competitive, one-upping flavor -- siblings outdoing each other's pranks. To surpass is loftier and wider: results can surpass forecasts, records, and expectations, not just other people.

outperform: To outperform is to deliver measurably better results than someone or something else -- a word at home in statistics, sales charts, and sports. To surpass is broader and grander: to go beyond a rival, a record, or what anyone expected.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fall short: to fail to reach a particular standard or level

lag behind: to fail to keep up with others in progress

Where it sits · how decisively the old mark is beaten — exceed → surpass → eclipse

exceed vs. surpass: Exceed is a bit more neutral than surpass -- exceed often describes simply going past a number or limit, while surpass emphasizes actively becoming better than a rival or previous record.

eclipse vs. surpass: Eclipse can feel more dramatic than surpass: surpass means going beyond a previous standard, while eclipse suggests completely overshadowing it, making the old standard seem small by comparison.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sur-

prefix — sur-: over, beyond (Latin (super-))

root — -pass-

root — -pass-: to step, pass (Latin (passus))

Put it together

Put it together: Sur- comes from Latin super, 'over' or 'beyond,' combined with pass, from Latin passus, 'a step.' To surpass something, at its root, is to step beyond it -- to go further than it did.

Use the root in a new word: trespass

Use the root in a new word: trespass: A sign warned hikers not to trespass onto the private farmland beyond the fence.
